name: Syriem
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Devi, Ashangbam Samani. 2015. Phonology of Syriem. Language in India 15(9): 84-94. Open access:http://www.languageinindia.com/sep2015/samanidevisyriemphonemicsfinal.pdf(Glottolog ref 660375)
catalog_locator: section 'Tone', journal pp. 92-93; syllable-structure statement journal pp. 84-85
catalog_quote: Syriem is a tonal language in which every syllable carries one of the three underlying tones. In isolation, three tones have been established: rising (low to high rise), falling (high to low fall) and low tone (fairly level but downslide before a pause). ... Low tone occurs in both open and closed syllables. ... Rising tone occurs both in open and closed syllable. [p. 92] ... Falling tone can occur with both open and closed syllables. [p. 93] ... Syriem words are largely monosyllabic. [p. 84]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Syriem is a tonal language in which every syllable carries one of the three underlying tones. In isolation, three tones have been established: rising (low to high rise), falling (high to low fall) and low tone (fairly level but downslide before a pause). The three tones are marked over the vowel, e.g. [ǎ]=rising tone, [â]=falling tone and [à]=low tone.
new_statements.citation: Devi, Ashangbam Samani. 2015. Phonology of Syriem. Language in India 15(9): 84-94.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (11 pp., text, Language in India 15:9, Sept 2015) opened and read in full. The quoted passage is present word for word under the heading "Tone": "Syriem is a tonal language in which every syllable carries one of the three underlying tones. In isolation, three tones have been established: rising (low to high rise), falling (high to low fall) and low tone (fairly level but downslide before a pause). The three tones are marked over the vowel, e.g. [ǎ]=rising tone, [â]=falling tone and [à]=low tone." Only difference from the report: the locator. The Tone heading and quote sit on PDF page 9, whose footer reads journal p. 92 (p. 8 / journal p. 91 is the vowel-phoneme page); the tone examples…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is given. The only prosodic statement is that Syriem is a tone language with three contrastive lexical tones (rising, falling, low) borne by every syllable; words are largely monosyllabic, with bisyllabic stems consisting of an (unstressed-looking, low-toned) prefix plus a root. The paper never uses the words 'stress' or 'accent'.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: in closed syllables with rising tone the coda is restricted to p, t, k, m, n, ŋ, l, r, y (p. 92); long vowels of open syllables shorten when compounded (p. 93).
new_statements.domain_note: Tones are described for syllables in isolation (citation forms); no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Devi 2015/2016 call the language Syriem (a.k.a. Fyriem); Deb & Debbarma 2012 call it Saihriem and describe it as 'one of the dialects of Hmar' (hmar1241), while Glottolog syri1242 treats it as a separate West/Old Kuki language 'closely related to Aimol' (aimo1244) and Haokip 2018/2019 record intelligibility claims with Hmar. Devi's data come from the same five Cachar villages (Balisor/Kuki Punji, Noksa/Nengpur, Bagbahar, Syriem Kho, Nagathol) that Wikipedia and Deb & Debbarma list for syri1242, so the quoted source is the language of record; note Devi describes it as a mixed Kuki-Chin koine (Aimol, Thadou clans, Kholang, Rangkhol, Tollai speakers).

new_statements.quote: Based on the two proposals above, Syriem is a tonal language in which every syllable carries one of the three underlying tones. In isolation, three tones have been established: rising (low to high rise), falling (high to low fall) and low tone (fairly level but downslide before a pause). [p. 63] ... Being a tonal language, tone is the most fundamental contrastive element in the suprasegmental phonology of Syriem. The tone occurs on the whole syllable as a unit, of which the vowel is the peak. The tonal analysis in this thesis is an auditory analysis based on recorded wordlists and text. There are three underlying tones in Syriem: low, rising, and falling. [p. 77]
new_statements.citation: Devi, Ashangbam Samani. 2016. A phonology of Syriem. PhD thesis, Assam University, Silchar (supervisor Pauthang Haokip), 144 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 6 'Tone', 6.1 Tone, thesis p. 63 = p. 1 (file, scanned in line 17ff); Conclusion chapter, Summary, thesis p. 77 = p. 2 (scanned in line 35ff; the scanned reads this file's heading as 'CHAPTER 6 CONCLUSION')

DEPARTMENT OF LINGUISTICS.. ASSAM UNIVERSITY SILCHAR-788011, INDIA 2015' = the cited Devi PhD thesis (catalog year 2016 = award/deposit year; Shodhganga hdl 10603/293372, the recorded_open_url); table of contents: Ch.3 Segmental Phonology p.18, Ch.4 Syllable Structure p.30 (4.1.1 Minor syllables p.33), Ch.5 Morphophonemics p.48, Ch.6 Tone p.63 (6.1.1 Rising, 6.1.2 Falling, 6.1.3 Low, 6.1.5 Tone dissimi…
new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same analysis as the catalog record (Devi 2015, Language in India 15(9): tonal, three tones rising/falling/low, no stress statement); the p. 63 sentence is word-for-word the catalog quote's source. The thesis adds tone dissimilation, tone sandhi, stem-tone alternations and a tone-distribution table but still says nothing about word stress, so the catalog classification tonal with no stress rule stands. Caveat on coverage: chapters 1-3, 5, ch.4 pp. 43-47, bibliography and annexure were saved but not scanned (no text), so a passing remark on stress there cannot be excluded; the contents list no such section.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Syriem is analysed as a tone language: every syllable bears one of three contrastive tones (rising, falling, low), established on monosyllables in isolation with minimal triplets (e.g. naa R 'fish', naa F 'five', naak L 'wait'); low tone shows two dissimilation patterns after low-tone proclitics, rising and falling tones undergo tone sandhi, low tone never does; tone-by-rhyme distribution restrictions are tabulated (Table 11). Word structure: mostly monosyllabic, up to four syllables, with prefixal minor (reduced) syllables before a major syllable. Nowhere in the tone chapter, the syllable/word-structure sections read, the conclusion or the table of contents is word stress, accent or prominence mentioned; the thesis makes no stress statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress statement of any kind)
new_statements.exceptions: tonal only: low-tone dissimilation after low-tone pronominal proclitics (ka 'my', ta 'your', a 'his/her'), tone sandhi affecting rising and falling tones but never low tone, three tone alternations between primary and secondary verb stems (rising tone never occurs in secondary stems; glottal stop associated with low tone); rhyme restrictions per tone (Table 11, p. 75)
new_statements.identity_note: Syriem (Saihriem) as spoken in the Barak Valley / Dima Hasao area of Assam (Devi's fieldwork variety per the 2015 article); the thesis record gives no further dialect detail.

tone_statements.citation: Haokip, Pauthang (data, 11 November 2011). Syriem (Fyriem), Assam, India. In: Chan, Eugene S. L. (ed.), Numeral Systems of the World's Languages. Leipzig: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology. Web page.
tone_statements.quote: In this thesis, we follow and agree with Devi (2015) in establishing three tones in Saihriem: rising, falling, and low. The tones are marked as follows: [ǎ]=rising tone, [ ]=falling tone and [à]=low tone. All the tones can occur in both open and closed syllables (as seen in the table below). … Low tones Rising tone Falling tone tàp ―cry‖ kǒ ―nine‖ thûu ―word‖ và ―bird‖ tsǒop ―suck‖ zôoŋ ―monkey‖ Table 4.3: Tones in Saihriem
tone_statements.locator: pp. 101-102, section 4.2.5 'Tone' (p. 101) and Table 4.3 'Tones in Saihriem' (p. 102)
tone_statements.summary: Three lexical tones in Saihriem: rising, falling and low, each found in open and closed syllables (following Devi 2015); tone marked with diacritics throughout; no word on downstep, sandhi or stress.
